{{Short description|Probability distribution used in multivariate hypothesis testing}}
In [[statistics]], '''Wilks' lambda distribution''' (named for [[Samuel S. Wilks]]), is a [[probability distribution]] used in [[Multivariate statistics|multivariate]] [[hypothesis testing]], especially with regard to the [[likelihood-ratio test]] and [[multivariate analysis of variance]] (MANOVA).

== Definitions ==
Wilks' lambda distribution is defined from two [[statistical independence|independent]] [[Wishart distribution|Wishart distributed]] variables as the [[ratio distribution]] of their [[determinant]]s,<ref name="MKB">
{{cite book
  | author = [[Kanti Mardia]], John T. Kent and John Bibby
  | title = Multivariate Analysis
  | publisher = Academic Press
  | year = 1979
  | isbn = 0-12-471250-9
}}</ref>

given

:<math>\mathbf{A} \sim W_p(\Sigma, m) \qquad \mathbf{B} \sim W_p(\Sigma, n)</math>

independent and with <math>m \ge p</math>

:<math>\lambda = \frac{\det(\mathbf{A})}{\det(\mathbf{A+B})} = \frac{1}{\det(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B})} \sim \Lambda(p,m,n)</math>

where ''p'' is the number of dimensions.  In the context of [[likelihood-ratio test]]s ''m'' is typically the error degrees of freedom, and ''n'' is the hypothesis degrees of freedom, so that <math>n+m</math> is the total degrees of freedom.<ref name="MKB"/>

== Properties ==
There is a symmetry among the parameters of the Wilks distribution,<ref name="MKB"/>
: <math>\Lambda(p, m, n) \sim \Lambda(n, m + n - p, p)</math>

=== Approximations ===
Computations or tables of the Wilks' distribution for higher dimensions are not readily available and one usually resorts to approximations.
One approximation is attributed to [[M. S. Bartlett]] and works for large ''m''<ref>
{{cite journal
  | author = [[M. S. Bartlett]]
  | title = A Note on the Multiplying Factors for Various <math>\chi^2</math> Approximations
  | journal = [[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society|J R Stat Soc Ser B]]
  | volume = 16 |issue=2
  | pages = 296–298
  | year = 1954
  | jstor = 2984057
}}
</ref> allows Wilks' lambda to be approximated with a [[chi-squared distribution]]
:<math>\left(\frac{p-n+1}{2}-m\right)\log \Lambda(p,m,n) \sim \chi^2_{np}.</math><ref name="MKB"/>

Another approximation is attributed to [[C. R. Rao]].<ref name="MKB"/><ref>{{Cite journal
 | author = [[C. R. Rao]]
 | title = An Asymptotic Expansion of the Distribution of Wilks' Criterion
 | journal = [[Bulletin de l'Institut International de Statistique]]
 | volume = 33 
 | year = 1951
 | pages = 177–180
}}</ref>

== Related distributions ==
The distribution can be related to a product of [[statistical independence|independent]] [[beta distribution|beta-distributed]] random variables
:<math>u_i \sim B\left(\frac{m+i-p}{2},\frac{p}{2}\right)</math>
:<math>\prod_{i=1}^n u_i \sim \Lambda(p,m,n).</math>
As such it can be regarded as a multivariate generalization of the beta distribution.

It follows directly that for a one-dimension problem, when the Wishart distributions are one-dimensional with <math>p=1</math> (i.e.,  chi-squared-distributed), then the Wilks' distribution equals the beta-distribution with a certain parameter set,
:<math>\Lambda(1,m,n) \sim B\left(\frac{m}{2},\frac{n}{2}\right).</math>

From the relations between a beta and an [[F-distribution]], Wilks' lambda can be related to the F-distribution when one of the parameters of the Wilks lambda distribution is either 1 or 2, e.g.,<ref name="MKB"/>
:<math>\frac{1 - \Lambda(p, m, 1)}{\Lambda(p, m, 1)} \sim \frac{p}{m - p + 1} F_{p, m-p+1},</math>
and
:<math>\frac{1 - \sqrt{\Lambda(p, m, 2)}}{\sqrt{\Lambda(p, m, 2)}} \sim \frac{p}{m - p + 1} F_{2p, 2(m-p+1)}.</math>
